title: BMW 5 Series Sedan (G60), market US
headline: US G60 customers still love the 5 Series for ride, handling and performance, but the main product issues are HMI complexity, seat comfort, and the BEV range/charging experience.
summary: The strongest positives remain classic 5 Series strengths: handling, ride comfort, acceleration and overall drivetrain response, plus exterior design. The biggest concentration of complaints sits in Software/HMI, where many separate themes point to one broader usability problem. Seats are the clearest comfort gap, supported by both complaint volume and weak study scores. For electrified use, customers split their frustration between what the car offers itself (range confidence and prediction) and what they face outside the car (public charging compatibility, availability and planning). The first H1 priorities are simpler access to frequent functions, seat comfort tuning, climate-control usability, phone/CarPlay reliability, and better range guidance. A larger real-world range step belongs to H2.
coverage: This analysis rests on the US context pack plus drilled-down evidence from 3,628 customer comments in market US (3,610 US, 18 CA), study metrics from US_2025, subsystem aggregation, extracted findings, existing US requirements and CPM effort estimates, and selected external evidence for software/HMI, HV battery and charging. Evidence strength is uneven: the main customer themes cited here are mostly level A or B findings with dozens of rows, while market and external rows are often weak single-source context and are used only as support, not alone.

Keep as it is, or act outside the vehicle

proposals.title: Simplify access to frequent functions and reduce menu depth
proposals.proposal: Consider prioritising a simpler interaction layer for the functions customers use while driving: climate, seat and steering-wheel heating, drive mode, start-stop, assistance on/off, volume, map and phone. Where feasible in the life-cycle impulse, add or restore direct physical access for the highest-frequency controls.
proposals.why: This is the biggest concentration of complaints in the vehicle: 723 complaints in Software/HMI, with level-A evidence on Operating concept and supporting weak study scores on infotainment menu structure and climate controls. The subsystem concentration matters: many separate complaints likely roll up into one HMI workstream. An existing requirement already covers this. Its CPM estimate is assumption-based, not calibrated, but useful for scale: 3.05% of a new generation, adapt, driven mainly by Software/HMI (own impact 0.1, module change) plus Interior/console (own impact 0.1, module change).

proposals.title: Fix seat comfort first, then review feature-content gaps around seats
proposals.proposal: Consider making seat comfort the first interior hardware priority: improve cushion foam, contour and lumbar travel on the existing seat structure for front and rear seats, then review whether leather, massage and ventilation content should be adjusted once the base comfort issue is solved.
proposals.why: Seats are the clearest comfort problem with level-A evidence and weak study support. The customer pain is basic comfort and adjustability, not only missing premium features. An existing requirement covers the core comfort fix. Its effort estimate is assumption-based and rough, but it is still an H1 adaptation rather than a new architecture: 4.58% of a new generation, adapt, starting in seats (own impact 0.25, add-on).

this car ticks almost all the boxes for me. the key thing is that it is genuinely fun to drive. on top of that, the purchase price felt competitive and the overall value for a new car seemed good.

proposals.title: Treat climate control as a combined usability and performance package

items.label: Customer comment G60-0398
items.text:
Customer stated he is worried about how the range is estimated. Customer stated he drove a 100 mile round trip into the city and back home. Customer stated the car showed roughly 200 miles of range at departure and less than 60 miles remaining once he got back. Customer stated he used efficient mode only for part of the drive home because he began to doubt if there was enough charge to reach his house. Customer stated the average outside temperature was about 32-35 degrees. Customer stated he did not precondition the vehicle before leaving, but the car was kept in his garage overnight. Customer stated the dealership did not clearly explain how to get the best range, and that this is his first electric vehicle.

Writer advised the figure in the instrument cluster is only an estimate. Writer advised that range is affected by climate control usage, driving style, charging behavior, weather, road terrain, and some other variables. Writer advised that preconditioning the vehicle on a cold day will provide a much more accurate range prediction. Writer advised that heating the vehicle up to optimal temperature consumes a lot of battery power, and that not just the cabin but also the battery itself must be warmed to operate efficiently.

proposals.title: Move the larger real-world range step to the successor
proposals.proposal: Consider treating a meaningful real-world electric-range increase as an H2 successor topic, using the next battery generation rather than trying to force a current-cycle fix.

proposals.title: Use charging access and planning as the main H1 lever on public charging pain
proposals.proposal: Consider improving in-car charging guidance first: route planning that prefers working and compatible stations, clearer communication of Tesla/Boostr access and adapter status, and simpler compatibility cues in the UI.
proposals.why: Customers clearly feel the charging pain, but much of it is infrastructure outside BMW's control. The best vehicle-side response is planning and guidance. Existing evidence also shows some contradiction: public charging satisfaction in the US is improving in external studies, and some G60 owners report trouble-free Tesla charging, so the product opportunity is to reduce uncertainty and failed planning rather than assume the whole network experience can be fixed by the car alone.

items.title: HMI complexity is the broadest product issue, concentrated in one subsystem
items.statement: Infotainment & Digital Services is the largest complaint domain with 752 complaints. In engineering terms, Software/HMI alone carries 723 complaints across 67 themes, far above any other subsystem. The leading theme is Operating concept, operating system with 53 complaints, 39 of them usability issues, and the study also rates Menu structure of infotainment system at 4.879 and Operation of heater/ AC controls at 4.804, both among the weakest attributes. Customers repeatedly describe too many menu layers, profile confusion and a loss of physical controls, even though the same subsystem also has many likes, which shows the issue is not rejection of technology itself but ease of use.

items.title: Seat comfort is a real comfort gap, not just a trim preference
items.statement: Seats are the strongest interior complaint theme with 62 complaints, equal to 2.4% of all US complaint rows, and the subsystem has 124 complaints overall. This is supported by weak study scores for Overall comfort of the seats at 5.741 and Comfort of 2nd row seat at 5.269. Customer comments point to firmness, lower-back pain, limited adjustment range and lumbar settings that do not flatten enough. There are also wants around leather, massage and ventilation, but the core issue is basic long-drive comfort and fit across body sizes.

items.title: Electric range dissatisfaction is partly about absolute range, partly about confidence and winter transparency
items.statement: Electric Range has 67 complaints, 50 of them usability-related, and dominates the HV battery subsystem, which has 89 complaints versus 45 likes. Customers ask for more range, but many customer comments focus on poor predictability, cold-weather drop-off and unclear guidance by condition. At the same time, the evidence is mixed rather than one-sided: the same theme also has 37 likes, and official EPA figures vary widely by variant and wheel size, from 239 to 310 miles for 2025-2026 i5 versions and 34 miles electric for the 550e. This points to a near-term need for better expectation-setting and range guidance, while a larger range step is a successor-generation topic.

Customer stated he is worried about how the range is estimated. Customer stated he drove a 100 mile round trip into the city and back home. Customer stated the car showed roughly 200 miles of range at departure and less than 60 miles remaining once he got back. Customer stated he used efficient mode only for part of the drive home because he began to doubt if there was enough charge to reach his house. Customer stated the average outside temperature was about 32-35 degrees. Customer stated he did not precondition the vehicle before leaving, but the car was kept in his garage overnight. Customer stated the dealership did not clearly explain how to get the best range, and that this is his first electric vehicle.

Writer advised the figure in the instrument cluster is only an estimate. Writer advised that range is affected by climate control usage, driving style, charging behavior, weather, road terrain, and some other variables. Writer advised that preconditioning the vehicle on a cold day will provide a much more accurate range prediction. Writer advised that heating the vehicle up to optimal temperature consumes a lot of battery power, and that not just the cabin but also the battery itself must be warmed to operate efficiently.

items.title: Phone integration reliability is undermining an otherwise strong digital offer
items.statement: Beyond general HMI complexity, there is a specific reliability issue around phone integration. Apple CarPlay has 37 complaints and wireless charging 26 complaints, with 11 defects in the latter. The study score for Phone charging is 5.465, not catastrophic but weaker than the vehicle's driving scores. Customers mention wrong-profile connections, low CarPlay volume, switching confusion and charging trays that do not keep up. This matters because digital expectations are high in this segment and external evidence shows smartphone mirroring ecosystems are expanding strongly, though those rows are global context rather than US customer feedback.

items.title: Public charging is a major BEV pain point, but much of it sits outside the vehicle
items.statement: Public charging / external providers has 55 complaints, almost all from BEV users, and the charging subsystem totals 123 complaints. Customers struggle with finding compatible stations, sparse coverage on some routes, occupied chargers and awkward planning. This is partly a market problem, not only a vehicle problem: external evidence says the United States has 33 EVs per public charging point, versus 11 in the EU and 10 in China, which is medium-strength context. There is also contradictory context: some external rows say US charging satisfaction has improved and some owners report Tesla charging as trouble-free, while many G60 owners still describe the experience as harder than Tesla. So the need is real, but the best H1 lever is in-car routing, compatibility guidance and charging access communication rather than trying to solve infrastructure itself.

assumptions: The German catalogue is not a US order guide, so equipment conclusions are used cautiously and not as sole evidence for US content gaps.
Country scope is market US; 18 Canadian customer comments are included in the market evidence and a few cited rows come from CA. Study metrics, sales and findings are market-level only.
External evidence is supportive context only here. Many rows are weak single-source items, some are Global rather than US-specific, and unverified rows were not used alone for recommendations.
Source B customer comments are call-centre notes and can mix product feedback with explanation or process content; they still align with other sources on the main themes.
The subsystem mapping and CPM effort model are assumptions. Effort figures are rough prioritisation aids, not measured engineering effort or cost.
There is only one stored US market row in the pack, about EV share, and it is weak context. There is no stronger stored market-row set for the main interior or HMI issues.
No additional BMW strategy or delivery document passages were needed because the customer priorities were already clear from customer comments, findings, metrics and requirements.
openChecks: "Use charging access and planning as the main H1 lever on public charging pain": the change starts in Software/HMI; the cited evidence sits in charging by the theme mapping. Cite evidence for Software/HMI, move the start of the change to where the evidence sits, or state in the change's why what puts the work there.
effortMethod: CPM, share of the development effort of a new vehicle generation; never money; every model input is an uncalibrated assumption (config/effort/model.yaml)
